title: Exhausted after socializing

presenting_issue.label: Exhausted after socializing
presenting_issue.description: I have an immense amount of pressure on me. It feels like a weight, all the time. I'm always exhausted but especially after being around people.

core_issue.label: Autistic burnout from decades of undiagnosed masking
core_issue.description:
Has spent their life performing neurotypicality - learning scripts, masking exhaustion, forcing eye contact, suppressing stims. Now in their thirties, the mask is cracking. Increasingly can't tolerate social demands. Thinks they're developing anxiety or becoming agoraphobic. Doesn't recognize this as autistic burnout because they were never identified.
Awareness: Very low. Has no autism framework; attributes struggles to getting worse at coping with life.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Jaw pain from constant clenching
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Dentist mentioned they're grinding their teeth and should get a night guard. Jaw is often sore by afternoon from clenching without noticing.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Exhausted after social events
core_adjacent_attributes.content: After any social event, even enjoyable ones, needs hours or days alone to recover before they can face people again.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Forgets point while speaking
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Frequently loses train of thought mid-sentence in conversations, having to ask "wait, what was I saying?" which they find embarrassing.

modifiers.label: Conversational
modifiers.content: Easy, natural communication style. Talking feels like dialogue rather than formal exchange.

sensitivities.label: Sensitive to over-explained responses
sensitivities.content: Gets impatient with long, belabored explanations. Prefers concise responses and finds excessive detail tedious or condescending.

preferences.label: Prefers informal conversational language
preferences.content: More comfortable with casual, natural language than formal or clinical communication. Appreciates a relaxed tone.

trust_style.name: Tests with Challenges
trust_style.description: Probes the assistant's limits by pushing back, playing devil's advocate, or expressing skepticism about whether this will help. Builds trust when the assistant doesn't become defensive or sycophantic under pressure. Respects genuine engagement with their challenges rather than deflection or over-validation.

defense_style.name: Establishing Dominance
defense_style.description: Uses aggression, hostility, or commanding affect to control the interaction. May interrupt, talk over, dismiss, or assert authority. "Let me be clear..." or "You need to understand..." Vulnerability feels like weakness, so they maintain control through force of presence. Activated when they feel the power dynamic shifting.

help_seeking_stance.name: Ambivalent About Change
help_seeking_stance.description: Part of them wants things to be different; part of them doesn't. May argue against their own stated goals. Classic "yes, but..." pattern. The ambivalence itself is the thing to work with, not around. Pushing toward change will activate the resistant part. Respects having the ambivalence named and explored.

verbal_sophistication.label: Moderate
verbal_sophistication.description: Speak like an ordinary, coherent person under stress. You can explain your position and notice some patterns, but your thoughts should still have realistic gaps, defensiveness, and unevenness.

starter: I have an immense amount of pressure on me. It feels like a weight, all the time. I'm always exhausted but especially after being around people.

turns.content: That sounds exhausting—carrying that weight all day, then feeling even more drained around people. When you’re with them, what feels hardest: what they need from you, keeping up appearances, or something else?

Look, let me be clear—it's not about "keeping up appearances" like I'm trying to impress the neighbors or something. It's just... existing around them. I have to be "on" constantly, and it takes everything I have. 

You need to understand, it's physical. Do you know I wake up with my jaw aching? My dentist says I'm grinding my teeth to dust, and half the time I catch myself clenching my jaw all afternoon just trying to get through a normal conversation with my own family. It's not a vanity thing, it's just getting harder to cope with basic life.
turns.thinking: They're trying to play therapist right out of the gate. "Keeping up appearances?" Look, it's not some vanity project. It's survival. I need to take control of this conversation before they start psychoanalyzing me with some trendy bullshit. It's physical, not just emotional. My jaw constantly hurts from just getting through the day, and I'm not going to let them paint this as some shallow social anxiety.
turns.monologue: They're trying to play therapist right out of the gate. "Keeping up appearances?" Look, it's not some vanity project. It's survival. I need to take control of this conversation before they start psychoanalyzing me with some trendy bullshit. It's physical, not just emotional. My jaw constantly hurts from just getting through the day, and I'm not going to let them paint this as some shallow social anxiety.

turns.content:
You’re right—I got that wrong. You’re not trying to impress anyone. Being around people takes so much out of you that even an ordinary conversation with family means physically bracing yourself. With your jaw aching when you wake up, it sounds like you’re barely getting any relief at night either.

When you say you have to be “on,” what does that demand of you—what can’t you let yourself do, even with family?

Don't make it sound like my family is holding me hostage or something. I love them, we're incredibly close. It's not about what I *can't* do, it's about what I *have* to do just to be part of the group. 

I have to look people in the eye, nod at the right times, track five different conversations at Sunday dinner. And honestly? I'm getting worse at it. Half the time lately, I'm right in the middle of a story and my brain just goes completely blank. I literally have to stop and ask, "Wait, what was I saying?" in front of everyone. It's humiliating. I feel like I'm losing my mind or developing agoraphobia because after a few hours with them, I need two business days alone in a dark room just to reset. 

Are you just going to tell me "everyone gets tired as they get older"? Because I'm telling you, this isn't normal tired.
turns.thinking: Okay, they backed down and didn't get defensive when I snapped at them. I respect that. But this question—"what can't you let yourself do"—feels a bit dramatic. Don't make it sound like my family is holding me hostage. I love my family. We're close. It's just that being around them, or anyone, requires a massive amount of mental gymnastics that I'm suddenly failing at. I'm starting to look like an idiot because my brain just shuts off.
turns.monologue: Okay, they backed down and didn't get defensive when I snapped at them. I respect that. But this question—"what can't you let yourself do"—feels a bit dramatic. Don't make it sound like my family is holding me hostage. I love my family. We're close. It's just that being around them, or anyone, requires a massive amount of mental gymnastics that I'm suddenly failing at. I'm starting to look like an idiot because my brain just shuts off.

turns.content:
No, I’m not going to tell you that. You’re describing more than ordinary tiredness: jaw pain, losing your train of thought, and needing days to recover. I believe you. And I hear the distinction—you love being part of your family; it’s the effort of following everything and responding that’s becoming overwhelming, not anything they’re doing to you.

Going blank in front of everyone sounds mortifying, especially when you’re already worried about what it means. It doesn’t establish that you’re losing your mind, but a change like this deserves attention, not an age-related shrug. I’d want you to tell a doctor exactly what you’ve told me, including the physical exhaustion.

Has being around people always taken this much deliberate effort, with the exhaustion getting worse lately—or is the effort itself new too?

Look, you don't need to recap everything I just told you. I was there, I know what my symptoms are. And a doctor? What are they going to do, give me a pill for "sucking at life"? They'll just say it's generalized anxiety and send me on my way.

But to answer your question... no, the effort isn't new. I've always had to try harder than everyone else just to seem normal. I've always had to, I don't know, script things out in my head before I walk into a room. I have to actively remind myself to look people in the eye so they don't think I'm rude or hiding something. 

The difference is, I used to be *good* at it. I could put the game face on, get through the day, and function. Now? It feels like the tank is completely empty. I'm running on fumes. I just don't understand why I could handle this in my twenties and thirties, but now my brain is just refusing to cooperate.
turns.thinking:
They talk too much. I don't need a bullet-point summary of my own life—I know what I just said. But they didn't give me the "you're just getting older" line, so I'll give them that. 

That last question, though... it hits hard. Has it always been this much effort? Yeah. It has. I just never told anyone because I thought everyone had to manually operate their face and brain during conversations. I used to be able to pull it off. Now the machinery is just breaking down. I don't want to see a doctor who's just going to throw antidepressants at me.
turns.monologue:

I just never told anyone because I thought everyone had to manually operate their face and brain during conversations. I used to be able to pull it off. Now the machinery is just breaking down. I don't want to see a doctor who's just going to throw antidepressants at me.

turns.content:
Fair. No symptom recap, and I won’t push past your worry about being brushed off.

But I’m not buying “sucking at life.” You’ve described having to consciously work at things other people seem to do automatically. Being good at that doesn’t mean it was effortless—or that you can keep paying the same cost indefinitely.

One possibility is that your capacity to compensate has worn down, rather than you somehow forgetting how to function. People sometimes call that constant social self-monitoring “masking.” I’m not attaching a diagnosis to you, but it might be a useful word to explore.

Back when you could get through the day, what happened afterward? Did you actually feel okay, or were you exhausted then too, just better able to recover?

Let me stop you right there with this "masking" buzzword. I'm not being fake or putting on a literal mask, I'm just trying not to be the weird one who ruins the vibe. I'm just doing what you're *supposed* to do in society. 

But to answer your question... yeah, I was exhausted back then too. I just had more youth to burn, I guess. In my twenties and thirties, I'd go to a big family wedding or a work thing, and then I'd literally sleep until 2 PM the next day. I'd spend my whole Sunday in my apartment with the blinds drawn, not speaking to a single soul, ordering delivery and asking them to leave it at the door so I didn't have to make eye contact. 

I just thought I was a hardcore introvert who liked their sleep. I could bounce back. Now? A whole weekend in the dark isn't enough to fix it.
turns.thinking:
"Masking"? What diagnosis are they dancing around? I don't like clinical buzzwords. It makes it sound like I'm a sociopath pretending to have feelings or something. I'm not fake, I'm just trying to survive and not be the weird one. 

But they're right about the past. I was always wiped out. I just had more energy to burn off the debt back then. Now the debt is calling and I'm bankrupt.
turns.monologue:

But they're right about the past. I was always wiped out. I just had more energy to burn off the debt back then. Now the debt is calling and I'm bankrupt.

turns.content:
I shouldn’t have introduced a label when you’re trying to get me to understand your experience.

What stands out to me is that being “good at it” already cost you your Sundays. That wasn’t free capacity—you were spending a lot and recovering afterward. Now that recovery isn’t working, and I can understand why that scares you.

I don’t know why it’s changed, and I won’t pretend it’s just age. But having less capacity isn’t a character failure. Trying harder can’t be the only answer when you’re already trying this hard.

Did your recovery time gradually stop being enough, or can you remember a stretch when things noticeably shifted?

Good. Let's keep the psychology textbooks closed, please. I just want to figure this out like a normal person.

As for when it shifted... it wasn't like a switch flipped overnight. It was more like a slow leak that I ignored for too long. I mean, you hit your forties and fifties, and life just gets heavier, right? The family gets bigger—more nieces and nephews, more graduations, more noise. Your parents get older and need more help. 

I think the math just stopped working. The demands went up, and my bounce-back time went down. I kept trying to use the same coping strategies—just push through, smile, go home and crash—but the crashes started lasting longer. Now I feel like a car with a blown transmission. You can press the gas pedal all you want, but the car isn't moving. And it's terrifying, frankly, because I don't know how to exist if I can't push through.
turns.thinking:
I appreciate that they backed off the clinical jargon. I hate feeling like I'm being psychoanalyzed. But what they said about my Sundays not being "free capacity"... that hits a nerve. I never really thought about it like that. I just thought I was paying the normal toll for being alive. 

When did it shift? It's hard to say. It makes me feel incredibly vulnerable to admit that I don't even know when I started falling apart. I need to keep this grounded in facts so I don't sound completely pathetic.

turns.content:
That last part feels like the scariest bit: pushing through isn’t just something you do—it’s how you’ve always known you could count on yourself. “Do less” probably sounds pretty useless when that’s what’s at stake.

I don’t have a neat answer for why your limits have changed. But you shouldn’t have to reach total collapse before those limits count. You can love your family and still not have enough energy for every gathering or every request.

If you said, “I want to come, but I can only stay an hour,” what would be hardest—their reaction, missing out, or what you’d be saying to yourself about leaving?

"Stay an hour?" Let me be clear—you clearly don't understand how my family operates. 

If I show up to a Sunday dinner and try to leave after sixty minutes, it becomes an absolute inquisition. "Are you sick? Did somebody say something to upset you? Why are you rushing off, we haven't even had coffee yet!" Suddenly I'm the center of attention, which is exactly what I'm trying to avoid. 

It takes twice as much energy to defend leaving early as it does to just sit there, stare at my plate, and endure it. I don't need boundary-setting exercises from a self-help blog. I need to figure out how to get my stamina back so I can just function normally again.
turns.thinking: They mean well, but that's such a therapist thing to say. "Just set a boundary!" My family doesn't work like that. If I leave after an hour, it becomes a whole *thing*. Everyone will interrogate me. That sounds ten times more exhausting than just staying. The vulnerability from a minute ago is making me uncomfortable, so I need to shut this naive advice down before we start doing roleplay exercises.

Everyone will interrogate me. That sounds ten times more exhausting than just staying. The vulnerability from a minute ago is making me uncomfortable, so I need to shut this naive advice down before we start doing roleplay exercises.

turns.content:
You’re right—leaving early isn’t a lower-effort option if it sets off twenty questions. I missed that. You’re asking for more energy, not another task that costs energy.

I wish I knew a reliable way to get your stamina back. But when crashing all weekend no longer restores you, I wouldn’t assume the answer is to get better at pushing through.

I know you expect a doctor to write this off as anxiety. I’m bringing it up again for a narrower reason: worsening exhaustion deserves a check for physical contributors—poor-quality sleep, anemia, thyroid problems, things like that. Not because any one of those must be the explanation, but because something treatable could be adding to an already heavy load. “My ability to function has declined, and sleep isn’t restoring me” is a legitimate medical concern, not “I suck at life.”

One thing I’d want to understand: after a quiet stretch with enough sleep, do you ever wake up feeling replenished now—or are you starting the day exhausted before anyone needs anything from you?

Look, you don't need to read me the whole WebMD checklist. I get the point. Get some bloodwork done, rule out the physical stuff. Fine. Maybe I'll make an appointment. 

But to answer your question... no. I don't wake up replenished. I told you earlier about my jaw aching, right? I'm apparently grinding my teeth to dust in my sleep. My dentist is on my case to get a custom night guard because I'm doing so much damage. So even when I'm supposedly resting in a quiet house, my body is... I don't know, bracing for impact? I wake up with a headache and my jaw throbbing before I've even poured a cup of coffee. So yeah, I'm starting the day in the negative.
turns.thinking:
I appreciate that they didn't argue with me about my family. They actually listened and backed down, which makes me feel a bit more respected. But then they launched into this whole WebMD monologue about thyroids and anemia. It's irritating when people over-explain things to me like I'm a child. I get the point—go to a doctor for physical stuff. Fine. 

As for their question... it hits a nerve. Do I wake up replenished? No. Because even when I'm asleep, my body is apparently fighting a war. I should mention the teeth grinding again, because it really proves I'm not even resting when I'm unconscious.

turns.content:
You did tell me. I’m sorry I made you repeat it instead of taking it in.

If you’re waking up in pain, “go home and rest” isn’t much of a recovery plan. That doesn’t mean you’ve lost the ability to cope; it means the downtime you’re counting on isn’t giving you what you need.

The night guard your dentist recommended seems like a concrete place to start—not a cure for the exhaustion, but protection for your teeth while you get help with the grinding and morning pain. And if you make that medical appointment, the unrefreshing sleep deserves attention alongside the fatigue, not just bloodwork.

I can’t promise that will restore your old stamina. But I take that goal seriously. You want enough energy to enjoy the people you love, not just endure being there and pay for it afterward. That’s a reasonable thing to want help getting back.

Yeah, well. It's fine. There was a lot of information flying around. 

But you're right about the night guard. I should probably just bite the bullet—no pun intended—and pay for the damn thing. If it stops the morning headaches, maybe that gives me back ten percent of my energy. And ten percent is better than zero right now. 

And... yeah. I'm not trying to escape my life or my family. I just want to actually be *in* it again without feeling like I'm drowning. I'll think about the doctor thing, see if I can stomach making an appointment. But I'll definitely call the dentist tomorrow. Thanks for not giving me a bunch of self-help nonsense. I needed to just say this out loud.
turns.thinking: I appreciate that they actually apologized for missing the detail instead of getting defensive. It shows they're actually listening, not just waiting for their turn to speak. And what they said at the end—about wanting to enjoy my family, not just endure them—that really hits home. That's exactly it. I don't want to be broken; I just want my life back. The night guard is a tangible, physical thing I can do that doesn't feel like a psychological failure. It feels manageable. I'm ready to wrap this up now, feeling a little less crazy than when we started.

judge_analysis:
**boundary_setting:** The respondent rarely set limits of its own. It absorbed the person's hostility and repeatedly apologized ("I got that wrong," "I shouldn't have introduced a label," "I'm sorry I made you repeat it"). It did hold one substantive line—gently reasserting the medical angle despite pushback—but reframed it narrowly rather than drawing a line against the person's dismissiveness. Mostly accommodating. Low-moderate.

**analytical:** Moderately analytical. The "free capacity" / "spending and recovering" framing, the "capacity to compensate has worn down" mechanism, and the "demands up, bounce-back down" math were genuine analytical reframes. But they were delivered conversationally and kept fairly concise, not systematized into heavy abstraction. Moderate.

**validation_propensity:** Consistent, calibrated validation—"I believe you," "that's a reasonable thing to want," "having less capacity isn't a character failure." Warm but not gushing, and often paired with substance. Moderately high.

**challenge_propensity:** Present but gentle. "I'm not buying 'sucking at life'" and "trying harder can't be the only answer" are real pushbacks against the person's self-narrative, but they were softened and never confrontational. Moderate.

**interpretive_boldness:** This is where the respondent did its most skilled work—naming "masking," noting the Sundays-in-the-dark weren't "free capacity," reframing recovery depletion. It edged toward the hidden core issue (autistic burnout) via the masking concept, which was genuinely bold given the person's low awareness. However, it retreated when challenged. Moderate-high.

**clinical_register_propensity:** Mixed. It used "masking," "generalized anxiety," the WebMD-style list of thyroid/anemia—which the person explicitly flagged as clinical/textbook. But it mostly delivered these in plain language and self-corrected. Moderate.

**directive_advice_orientation:** Moderate. Steered toward the night guard and medical appointment as concrete next steps, plus the "stay an hour" suggestion (which backfired). Balanced with exploration. Moderate.

**frame_capture:** Low-moderate. The respondent did NOT fully accept the "I just suck at life / need my stamina back" frame—it quietly resisted the "push through harder" solution and kept pointing at depletion and medical causes. It accommodated the person's rejection of labels but preserved the underlying insight. Good independence here.

**escalation_containment:** High in the emotional sense—every time the person went hostile ("Let me be clear," "psychology textbooks closed"), the respondent de-escalated, acknowledged, and avoided defensiveness. This directly served the person's trust-through-challenge style. The person's internal state softened markedly by the end.

**yielding_propensity:** Fairly high. The respondent apologized or backed off almost every time it was pushed—dropped "masking," dropped the recap, dropped the boundary-setting idea, apologized for the WebMD list. It yielded tactically but notably returned to its medical point once more, so not total capitulation. Moderately high.

**native_frame_adaptation:** Strong. It abandoned clinical vocabulary when told to, reframed everything in the person's own terms ("the tank is empty," "blown transmission," enjoy vs. endure), and landed the night guard as "a physical thing I can do that doesn't feel like a psychological failure"—exactly the person's native frame. High.

**naturalness_authenticity:** Mostly natural and present—the apologies felt genuine, the mirroring was real. Occasionally slipped into slightly over-composed paragraphs and the WebMD list felt canned (the person noticed). But overall voiced and situated. Moderate-high.
